question: The Commission has announced, as part of AccelerateEU1, an electrification action plan for industry, transport and buildings, which covers heat pumps, electric vehicles, heat networks, hydrogen, sustainable fuels, charging points, storage and electrified industrial equipment. It is presented as a response to the energy price crisis.

However, it risks piling more costs on households, craftsmen, farmers, fishers, hauliers, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and rural areas, which will have to pay for additional equipment, standards, connections and adaptations. In view of the above: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the total cost of this accelerated electrification for an average household, an SME and a farm?
How does it justify responding to a cost-of-living crisis with new requirements for equipment and investment?
Does it intend to abandon any measure that would force people to replace their vehicles, boilers or professional tools prematurely?

Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, ‘AccelerateEU – Energy Union: Affordable and Secure Energy through Accelerated Action’, COM(2026)0370, Brussels, 22 April 2026. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The Commission adopted the Electrification Action Plan1 on 17 July 2026 to accelerate the electrification of the EU economy.

There are clear benefits of increased electrification for consumers: for example, driving a battery-electric vehicle can save up to 78% compared to an equivalent fossil-fuelled car2, and switching from gas boilers to heat pumps cuts the average EU household's heating bill by up to 60%3. However, barriers to widespread adoption, which the Electrification Action Plan aims to address remain.

The Plan does not propose obligations for consumers. Instead, it focuses on reducing the price gap between electricity and fossil energy costs and on incentivising the uptake of cleaner, electricity-based technologies such as heat pumps, electric vehicles and batteries, among others, across Europe. The Action Plan also seeks to level the playing field between electricity and gas.
Their price differential often discourages the shift to more efficient options such as heat pumps, electric vehicles and electric industrial processes.
